strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck in vision-language retrieval: costly online ViT feature extraction for joint-encoder rerankers.
Proposes a clear modular architecture: offline vision-token precomputation, lightweight adapter, compact MiniLM joint encoder, and optional token compression.
Reports useful efficiency-oriented measurements such as latency, storage per image, and ablation on number of compressed tokens.
Demonstrates consistent improvements over several embedding backbones on Flickr30k in Table 1, showing versatility as a drop-in reranker.
Shows data efficiency in comparison to BLIP-2 by using only 12M/14M training pairs instead of hundreds of millions.
Ablates several relevant design choices: token count, reranking pool size, training objectives, and distillation.
Hyperparameters and implementation details are documented, and code/checkpoints are promised, which supports reproducibility.
The paper is generally well written and the motivation is easy to follow.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: precomputing/caching vision tokens and compressing them with learnable query-based attention are well-known ideas from Q-Former, Perceiver-style attention pooling, ColBERT/ColPali, and VLM adapters. The paper largely combines existing components rather than introducing a fundamentally new method.

The central claim of matching or surpassing prior joint encoders is not supported by the reported numbers. For example, Table 2 shows EDJE Local ViT-L/16 at 87.8/96.5 Flickr R@1 versus BLIP-2 at 88.6/96.9, and 64.9/81.0 COCO-FT versus BLIP-2 at 66.3/83.5. This contradicts the abstract and contribution wording about matching prior art.

The comparison to prior art is confounded: EDJE uses SigLIP2 vision backbones while ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 use their original CLIP-style backbones. Gains may partly reflect stronger vision encoders rather than the reranking architecture itself.

Storage and inference comparisons are not cleanly apples-to-apples. Prior-art storage appears to be computed under different precision assumptions than EDJE, and the cached-vision regime excludes the very vision extraction stage that the paper identifies as the bottleneck for prior methods.

Despite the title and motivation around large-scale retrieval, evaluation is limited to Flickr30k and MS-COCO. There is no actual web-scale or million-candidate retrieval experiment, no end-to-end latency including disk I/O for cached tokens, and no evaluation with large reranking pools.

The throughput claim of 50k image-text pairs/second in the abstract is not supported by Table 2: 64 pairs in 1.91 ms corresponds to roughly 33.5k pairs/s, and the paper does not clearly specify the batch size or measurement protocol for the 50k figure.

There are technical inconsistencies in the training description. Section 4 lists image-text matching, masked language modeling, and text-embedding recovery as the three heads, but Table 4 ablates ITC instead of text-embedding recovery. The negative mining description also conflicts somewhat with Table A, which says 'Hard negatives: None'.
The evaluation lacks statistical significance tests, error bars, or multiple seeds, making it difficult to judge whether small differences are meaningful.
No efficient multimodal reranking baselines beyond the BLIP family are compared, and there is no controlled comparison using the same vision encoder for prior joint encoders.

The paper does not adequately analyze potential false negatives introduced by in-batch hard-negative mining using the embedding model, although this could affect discriminative training substantially.

The token-compression results mainly show a trade-off curve; the paper does not establish that the compressed variant is Pareto-optimal against simpler alternatives such as PCA, pooling, or storing FP16 full tokens.
Ethical and societal implications of large-scale multimodal retrieval/content moderation are not discussed, though this is a secondary concern relative to the technical and empirical issues.

strengths: Targets an important and practical problem: efficient vision-language reranking for large-scale retrieval.
The proposed EDJE architecture is simple and modular, combining frozen vision encoders with a compact language model and an attention-based token-compression adapter.
The efficiency results are promising: low per-image storage and fast joint-encoding inference compared to prior joint encoders.
The paper evaluates several vision backbones and includes ablations on token count, reranking pool size, and training objectives.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: precomputing vision features and compressing tokens with learnable queries is closely related to existing methods such as BLIP-2's Q-Former, ColBERT/ColPali-style late interaction, and attention pooling. The contribution is primarily an engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new method.

Overclaimed performance: the abstract and introduction claim 'matching prior art' on Flickr and COCO, but Table 2 shows EDJE is consistently below BLIP-2 on COCO and mostly below on Flickr, especially in compressed variants.

Unfair or misleading comparisons: EDJE freezes a SigLIP2 vision encoder trained on massive data, but Table 2 only counts joint-encoder training data, making the 'data-efficient' comparison to BLIP/BLIP-2 misleading. The comparison to BLIP-2 also uses much larger pretraining data and different architectures.

Evaluation is limited to small retrieval benchmarks (Flickr30k and COCO). No large-scale retrieval evaluation is provided despite the paper's central 'large scale' and throughput claims. There is no end-to-end latency/throughput evaluation on millions of images, no evaluation of storage/retrieval trade-offs at scale, and no error bars or multiple runs.

Technical and reproducibility issues: the training and offline preprocessing pipeline is not clearly explained, e.g., how the adapter is trained if it is applied offline, whether compressed tokens are recomputed, and how text embeddings are aligned across different text encoders. Key architecture details such as adapter depth, number of heads, MLP dimensions, and exact SigLIP2 variant are missing. Code and checkpoints are not yet available.

Numerical inconsistencies: Section 3.1 reports roughly 400 ms and 1400 ms for ViT feature extraction, while Table 2 reports 83 ms and 101 ms for BLIP inference; it is unclear whether Table 2 excludes ViT for all methods. The abstract's 50k pairs/second claim is not clearly supported by the reported 1.91 ms for 64 samples, which implies about 33.5k pairs/second.

Baselines and ablations are incomplete: there is no comparison to other compression or reranking approaches such as Q-Former variants, pooling, or late-interaction models under the same cached-vision regime; no ablation on language model size, adapter architecture, or number of queries beyond token count. The gains over strong embedding models like SigLIP2 are modest and may not justify the added complexity.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: beating embedding models by reranking top-k candidates is expected, and the paper does not show that similar gains cannot be obtained by simpler reranking or a stronger embedding model.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in multimodal retrieval: visual feature extraction dominates joint encoders. Precomputing vision tokens offline and compressing them is a sensible and effective direction.

EDJE is modular and efficient: it can pair any ViT with a small language model, and the token-compression adapter substantially reduces storage and online compute, achieving large speedups and low per-image storage compared with BLIP/BLIP-2.
Empirical results show consistent improvements over embedding models (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) on Flickr30k zero-shot retrieval, demonstrating usefulness as a drop-in reranker.
Competitive performance with ALBEF/BLIP on Flickr and COCO while using a much smaller joint encoder (33M vs 139-167M parameters) and less training data (12M vs 129M/400M).
Ablations on token count, reranking pool size, training objectives, and distillation provide useful insights into design choices.
Reproducibility details are mostly provided: hyperparameters, training data mixture, and evaluation protocol are described, and code/checkpoints are promised.
weaknesses: The central claim of matching prior art is overstated. Table 2 shows EDJE (even local ViT-L) is below BLIP-2 on all reported Flickr/COCO metrics, especially COCO image-to-text (81.0 vs 83.5), and compressed variants are lower still. The abstract's claim of matching prior art on COCO is not fully supported.

Evaluation is limited to Flickr30k and COCO (1k/5k images) with small reranking pools (default k=10). Despite 'large scale' in the title, no large-scale retrieval benchmark or end-to-end retrieval including first-stage search and disk I/O is evaluated.

Comparison fairness is questionable: EDJE uses SigLIP2, a stronger and more recent vision backbone, while ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 use CLIP/EVA-style backbones. This confounds joint-encoder gains with vision backbone quality. Storage comparisons may also mix precision/dimensionality (e.g., FP16 vs FP32) and need clarification.

Novelty is moderate: precomputing visual tokens, projecting them into a small LM, and compressing them via attention-based queries closely resemble existing late-interaction, VLM projection, and Q-Former/attention-pooling mechanisms. The paper does not sufficiently differentiate its technical contribution from these prior works.

Inconsistencies reduce confidence: the abstract reports 50k pairs/s but Table 2 implies roughly 33.5k pairs/s (64 / 1.91 ms). Training objectives are named inconsistently (text-embedding recovery vs. ITC; hard-negative mining vs. Table 3 'Hard negatives: None').
Code/checkpoints are not yet available at review time, and broader ethical/broader-impact considerations for retrieval systems (bias, privacy, surveillance) are not discussed.
Some formatting and writing issues (e.g., 'To goal of this section', broken table formatting, reference typos) slightly affect clarity.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important bottleneck in vision-language re-ranking: costly online visual feature extraction, which prevents joint encoders from being deployed at scale.
Proposes a clear efficiency-oriented design: precompute vision tokens offline, compress them with a lightweight attention-based adapter, and run only a compact MiniLM joint encoder online.
Reports consistent retrieval gains over multiple embedding backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) on Flickr30k zero-shot retrieval.

Achieves competitive performance against BLIP/BLIP-2 on Flickr30k and COCO while using much less training data, a far smaller joint encoder, lower online latency, and 49kB per-image storage in the compressed variant.

Provides extensive supporting analyses: token-count ablations, re-ranking pool-size robustness, training-objective ablations, distillation, token-compression baselines, quantization, full-dataset retrieval, and interpretability of compressed tokens.
The paper is well structured and mostly reproducible, with detailed hyperparameters, pseudo-code, and publicly released code.
weaknesses: The abstract's headline claim of processing 50k image-text pairs/second is not supported by Table 2: the 64-token compressed model takes 1.91 ms for a batch of 64, i.e. roughly 33.5k pairs/second, not 50k. This weakens the central efficiency claim.

The claim of 'matching prior art' on COCO fine-tuned retrieval is overstated: EDJE local ViT-L reports 64.9/81.0 T2I/I2T versus BLIP-2's 66.3/83.5, a non-trivial gap, especially for image-to-text retrieval.

Novelty is moderate: the proposed token-compression adapter is closely related to Q-Former/Perceiver-style attention pooling, and the broader idea of precomputing vision features is a natural system design choice. The paper lacks a direct Q-Former-style compression baseline.

Evaluation is limited to Flickr30k and COCO. The full-dataset retrieval experiments compare only against LightningDOT, an older baseline, and do not include BLIP/BLIP-2 or modern embedding models under the same protocol.

The cached-vision comparison in Table 2 may be somewhat favorable to EDJE: prior methods' storage is reported in FP32 and at their native feature dimension, while EDJE stores FP16 tokens projected to MiniLM's 384-dimensional space. The fairness of this comparison should be clarified.

The method relies heavily on a strong negative miner: using a weaker CLIP miner for a SigLIP2-based EDJE degrades performance substantially. This limits the practical generality and adds dependence on the underlying embedding model.

End-to-end latency including token I/O is not integrated into the main claims. Appendix C.1 estimates I/O overhead, but the combined throughput may be lower than the abstract's claim once storage reads are included.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: online visual feature extraction dominates inference cost in vision-language joint encoders for re-ranking.
Proposes a sensible architecture (EDJE) that precomputes vision tokens offline and compresses them via a lightweight attention-based adapter, reducing storage and online compute.

Modular design allows pairing different vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) with a small language model (MiniLM), and experiments show consistent improvements over embedding-only baselines on Flickr30k.
Provides useful efficiency analysis: per-image storage, joint-encoder parameter count, and inference time comparisons to ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 under a cached-vision regime.
Includes ablations on token compression, training objectives, pool size, quantization, full-dataset retrieval, and some interpretability analysis; code and training details are provided.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation inconsistency: with a fixed top-k=10 re-ranking pool, R@10 must be invariant, yet Table 1 reports changes in R@10 (e.g., CLIP ViT-B/16 T2I R@10 91.8→91.7; CLIP ViT-L/14 3362 I2T R@10 99→99.9). This is mathematically impossible and suggests misreported results or an unclear retrieval protocol, undermining the main retrieval gains.

Comparison to prior joint encoders is confounded: EDJE uses SigLIP2 ViT-L/16, while ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 use weaker CLIP/ViT backbones. The reported competitiveness may come from the stronger vision encoder rather than the proposed architecture. A controlled comparison with the same backbone is missing.

Efficiency claims are not fully supported: the abstract claims 50k image-text pairs/second, but Table 2 reports ~33.5k pairs/s (64 / 1.91 ms) for the compressed variant. Inference times for the local 576-token variant (2.86–4.14 ms for batch 64) also appear inconsistent with MiniLM-L12 compute.

Novelty is limited: token compression with learnable queries is closely related to Q-Former/Perceiver-style attention pooling; precomputing visual tokens is standard in late-interaction retrieval; the training objectives (ITM, MLM, text-embedding recovery, distillation) are largely standard. The contribution is mainly an engineering combination.

The paper overstates its results: on COCO fine-tuned retrieval, EDJE is slightly below BLIP/BLIP-2 (e.g., T2I 64.9 vs 66.3), and the comparison is confounded. Claims of 'surpasses or matches' are stronger than the evidence.
Evaluation is narrow: only Flickr30k and COCO retrieval are used. No larger-scale retrieval benchmarks or other tasks (e.g., zero-shot classification, VQA) are evaluated to demonstrate generality.
Interpretability and alignment analyses are qualitative or use metrics not directly optimized for retrieval; their connection to downstream performance is weak.
Some reproducibility details are missing (exact negative sampling procedure, how storage/inference times are measured, training data mixture specifics), making independent verification difficult.

strengths: Addresses a real and important bottleneck in vision-language retrieval: the expensive online visual feature extraction stage of joint encoders. Precomputing vision tokens offline and compressing them with a lightweight adapter is a practical and well-motivated design.

The EDJE architecture is efficient: it uses a small MiniLM joint encoder and a token-compression adapter, reducing joint-encoder parameters (33M vs 139M-167M for prior art), online latency (2-4 ms vs 45-100 ms for a batch of 64), and per-image storage (49-98 kB vs 1.7-2.4 MB).

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2), zero-shot Flickr30k, fine-tuned COCO, full-dataset retrieval, ablations on training objectives, token compression, pool size, quantization, text encoder, and negative mining. The results show consistent improvements over embedding baselines and competitive performance with prior joint encoders using far less training data.

Practical deployment considerations are well covered: pseudo-code for indexing/retrieval, I/O benchmarks for fetching precomputed tokens, interpretability analysis of compressed tokens, and quantization studies. Reproducibility is supported by hyperparameters and public code.
The token-compression adapter outperforms simple compression baselines such as striding, clustering, and attention pruning, demonstrating the effectiveness of the learned query-based compression.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the architecture combines existing ideas—frozen vision encoder, projection/adapter, small language model, attention-based token compression similar to Q-Former/Perceiver, and re-ranking. The main contribution is a system-level efficient design rather than a fundamentally new method.

The central efficiency claim of '50k image-text pairs/second' is not supported by Table 2. With a batch of 64 and 1.91 ms for Compressed-64, throughput is roughly 33.5k pairs/s; the discrepancy should be explained or the claim corrected.

The abstract claims 'matching prior art on Flickr (zero-shot) and COCO (fine-tuned) retrieval', but on COCO EDJE is lower than BLIP-2 (e.g., T2I R@1 64.9 vs 66.3; I2T 81.0 vs 83.5) and slightly lower than BLIP-L on I2T. It is competitive, but not matching state-of-the-art prior joint encoders.

Evaluation is limited to Flickr30k and COCO, which are small-scale (about 30k images). Despite the 'large-scale' framing, there is no true web-scale retrieval experiment over millions or billions of candidates. The I/O analysis is a useful step but not a full large-scale evaluation.

The comparison to prior joint encoders under the 'cached-vision regime' may not be entirely fair: storage for prior art appears to assume FP32 while EDJE uses FP16/BF16, and prior methods do not have a compression adapter. The cached-vision assumption is favorable to EDJE and should be discussed more carefully.

Some inconsistencies and unclear details: training data size is stated as 14M in Section 5.1 but 12M in Table 2; the training objective is called 'text-embedding recovery' in the main text but 'ITC' in Table 4; and it is unclear whether the adapter parameters are included in the reported 33M joint-encoder parameter count.

The paper does not compare against other efficient re-ranking or late-interaction vision-language models beyond ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2. Additional efficient re-ranker baselines would strengthen the claims.
